1. The present appeal has been filed under Section 374(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (
hereinafter, referred to as 'Cr.P.C.') against the judgment dated 29.06.2019 (hereinafter referred to as 'impugned judgment'), passed by the learned Metropolitan Magistrate/ Ld. MM-04, Central, Tis Hazari Courts, Delhi (hereinafter referred to as the 'Ld. Trial Court/Ld. MM Court') in case bearing "State v. Mustafa, Case No. 303810/2016", arising out of Challan No. 256247/2016, PS. SPCA,
convicting the appellant for the offence punishable under Section 11(d) of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 (hereinafter referred to as the 'PCA Act') and violation of Rules 47(a) and 54 of Transport of Animals Rules, 1978 ( hereinafter referred to as 'Rules/TA Rules') read with Section 38(2)/(3) of the PCA Act, and the consequent order of sentence dated 12.07.2019 (hereinafter referred to as 'impugned order'), passed by the Ld. (Rupees One Hundred only) for the violation/committing offence under Section 47(a) of TA Rules r/w Section 38(3) PCA Act; and imprisonment for a period 02 (two) months along with fine of Rs.

2. Succinctly, the case of the prosecution against the appellant is that on 11.06.2016, at around 03:15 a.m., at Ghazipur Chowk, Delhi within the jurisdiction of Delhi Society for Prevention of Cruelty to Animals/DSPCA, the appellant was found carrying/transporting 09 (nine) buffalo calves in a vehicle bearing registration no. DL-1LR-4358. Further, as per the prosecution, at such time, legs of said Mustafa Ali vs The State on 16 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/28980176/ 
1 animals were found tied as well as no arrangements for their food and water were found, besides no medical certificate of veterinary doctor in regard to such animals was produced by the appellants.
Accordingly, it was asserted that the animals were subjected to unnecessary pain and suffering,
leading to the initiation of the present proceedings. Accordingly, on the basis of the complaint/challan as well as upon hearing arguments on charge, addressed by/on behalf of the appellant as well as Ld. Addl. PP for the State, charges under Section 11(d) of PCA Act and Rules 47(a) and 54 of TA Rules read with Section 38(2) PCA Act were framed against the appellant by ABHISHEK GOYAL GOYAL Date:
2024.10.16 15:44:18 +0530 the Ld. Trial Court vide order dated 12.08.2016, to which the appellant pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. Relevantly, during the course of trial, prosecution examined 03 (three) witnesses, namely, Ct. Kavinder Pal (PW-1),
Ct. Naresh Kishore (PW-2), and Ct. Mahesh Kumar (PW-3). Subsequently, on conclusion of prosecution evidence, recording of statement of the appellant under Section 313/281 Cr.P.C. on 28.05.2019, as well as upon arguments being addressed by/on behalf of the appellant and State, as aforementioned, the Ld. Trial Court vide impugned judgment and order, while holding the appellant guilty of the offences punishable under Section 11(d) PCA Act and Rules 47(a) and 54 of TA Rules read with Section 38(2)/(3) PCA Act, sentenced him in the manner, as noted hereinabove. 
3. Learned Counsel for the appellant submitted that the impugned judgment and order were passed by the Ld. Trial Court, without application of mind, making the same illegal, unjustified and against all cannons of law. Ld. Counsel further submitted that the Ld. Trial Court, while passing the impugned judgment and order, failed to appreciate that no material and/or evidence was placed/brought before it, necessitating and/or validating the conviction of the appellant for any offence, leave aside, offences under Section 11(d) PCA Act and Rules 47(a) and 54 of TA Rules read with Section 38(2)/(3) PCA Act. In this regard, it was further submitted that in the absence of material and evidence, the Ld. Trial Court wrongly/erroneously relied upon the unproved facts and mistakenly convicted the appellant. Ld. Counsel further submitted that the Ld. Trial Court, while rendering the impugned judgment and order, not only ignored the facts before it, rather, also overlooked the settled position of law that in case, where two alternatives/views are equally possible,
court(s) must accept the ABHISHEK GOYAL GOYAL Date:
2024.10.16 15:44:22 +0530 view which is favorable to the accused. As per the Ld.
Counsel, the Ld. Trial Court has further disregarded the settled position of law that in a case where reasonable doubt arises regarding the guilt, benefit of the same cannot be withheld from an accused. 
4. Learned Counsel for the appellant further vehemently contended that the impugned judgment and order were passed by the Ld. Trial Court on mere conjunctures, surmises and in contravention of the settled principles of law, deserving their setting aside at the outset. In this regard, Ld. Counsel outrightly submitted that the Ld. Trial Court failed to appreciate that in the instant case, there are numerous gaping holes, infirmities, and contradictions in the testimonies of prosecution witnesses,
making the entire prosecution story unworthy of credence, not appealing to the senses of a prudent Mustafa Ali vs The State on 16 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/28980176/
2 man. It was further submitted by Ld. Counsel for the appellant that the Ld. Trial Court failed to appreciate the facts and circumstances of the case and even failed to consider the submissions of the appellant as well as erred in convicting the appellant. In this regard, Ld. Counsel, while referring to the testimony of PW-1/Ct. Kavinder Pal, contended that the said witness in his cross-examination,
explicitly deposed that he could not recollect where the appellant was apprehended along with the animals as well as asserted that the IO had not taken photographs of the loaded animals on the said vehicle, besides as per PW-1, the IO did not seize the 'so called ropes' with which the legs of the animals in question are affirmed to have been tied by the appellant. Accordingly, Ld. Counsel submitted that the possibility of animals being planted on the appellant by the concerned police officials/Investigating Officer cannot be ruled out. Correspondingly, as per Ld. Counsel for the appellant, PW-2/Ct. Naresh Kishore and PW-3/Ct. Mahesh Kumar, deposed variable ABHISHEK GOYAL GOYAL Date:
2024.10.16 15:44:26 +0530 places of alleged apprehension of the appellant. In this regard, Ld. Counsel accentuated that while as per PW-2, the appellant was allegedly apprehended at Shastri Park, Near Shastri Park Chowk, in contrast, PW-3 asserted that the appellant was apprehended from point between ISBT to Ghazipur. Ergo, as per the Ld. Counsel for the appellant, there are material contradictions in the testimonies of the said witnesses making the same grossly unreliable and unworthy of credence, basis which, as per the Ld. Counsel, no finding of guilt/conviction could have been reached by the Ld. Trial Court. Even otherwise, it was submitted by the Ld.
Counsel that no public witnesses were joined during the investigation, besides the seizure of so called 09 (nine) buffalo calves from the vehicle of appellant has not been proved by any cogent material/evidence by the prosecution. Further, it was submitted that no attempt was even made by the concerned investigating officer to retrieve CCTV footage of the alleged incident spot, which would have facilitated the Court in the ascertainment of the correct factual scenario of the case. Lastly, it was fervently reiterated by the Ld. Counsel that under such factual scenario, possibility of the alleged recovery being planted upon the appellant and the appellant being falsely implicated in the present case cannot be ruled out. Accordingly, Ld. Counsel submitted that the present appeal be allowed, by according benefit of doubt in favour of the appellant and the impugned orders be set aside. 
5. Per contra, Ld. Addl. PP for the State submitted that the impugned judgment and order was passed by the Ld. Trial Court after due appreciation of the facts and circumstances of the case as well as in consonance with the settled judicial precedents. Ld. Addl. PP for the State further submitted that the testimony of the witnesses brought forth on record are not only unblemished ABHISHEK GOYAL GOYAL Date:
2024.10.16 15:44:41 +0530 and consistent, rather, unerringly point out towards the only inference of guilt of the appellant. Further, as per the Ld. Addl. PP for the State,
omission of joining public witnesses, at the stage of apprehension and recovery from the appellant is not detrimental to the prosecution case, especially when the same stands duly proved from the consistent testimonies of witnesses adduced by the Mustafa Ali vs The State on 16 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/28980176/
3 prosecution. In fact, as per Ld. Addl. PP for the State, the testimonies of the prosecution witnesses have not only been consistent, rather, of sterling quality,
lucidly pointing out towards the only inference of guilt of the appellants. It was further submitted by the Ld. Addl. PP for the State that the appellants have even failed to prove its defence before the Ld. Trial Court by adducing any witnesses,
independent/uninterested witnesses. Accordingly, Ld. Addl. PP for the State submitted that the present appeal deserves to be dismissed at the outset, as grossly malicious and devoid of merits. 
6. The arguments of Ld. Counsel for the appellant as well as that of Ld. Addl. PP for the State have been heard and the record(s), including the Trial Court Record, thoroughly perused. 
7. Before proceeding further with the determination of the rival contentions of the parties, this Court deems it prudent to outrightly vocalize the scope of jurisdiction of this Court in an appeal. In this regard, this Court deems it prudent to make a reference to the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Padam Singh v. State of U.P., (2000) 1 SCC 621, wherein the Hon'ble Court, while delving into the issue of 'scope and ambit' of appellate court's jurisdiction inter alia noted as under;
"2. ... It is the duty of an appellate court to look into the evidence adduced in the case and arrive at an independent conclusion as to whether the said evidence can be relied upon or not and even if it can be ABHISHEK GOYAL GOYAL Date:
2024.10.16 15:44:55 +0530 relied upon, then whether the prosecution can be said to have been proved beyond reasonable doubt on the said evidence. The credibility of a witness has to be adjudged by the appellate court in drawing inference from proved and admitted facts. It must be remembered that the appellate court, like the trial court, has to be satisfied affirmatively that the prosecution case is substantially true and the guilt of the accused has been proved beyond all reasonable doubt as the presumption of innocence with which the accused starts, continues right through until he is held guilty by the final court of appeal and that presumption is neither strengthened by an acquittal nor weakened by a conviction in the trial court. The judicial approach in dealing with the case where an accused is charged of murder under Section 302 has to be cautious, circumspect and careful and the High Court,
therefore, has to consider the matter carefully and examine all relevant and material circumstances, before upholding the conviction." 
(Emphasis supplied) 
8. Similarly, the Hon'ble Apex Court in Narendra Bhat v. State of Karnataka, (2009) 17 SCC 785,
pronounced in respect of the foregoing as under;
"3. This Court has in a series of judgments held that a court exercising appellate power must not only consider questions of law but also questions of fact and in doing so it must subject the evidence to a critical scrutiny. The judgment of the High Court Mustafa Ali vs The State on 16 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/28980176/
4 must show that the Court really applied its mind to the facts of the case as particularly when the offence alleged is of a serious nature and may attract a heavy punishment." 
(Emphasis supplied) 
9. Markedly, from a conjoint reading of the aforenoted judicial dictates it can be perspicuously deduced that the jurisdiction of this Court in an appeal extends to re-appreciation of the entire material placed on record of the trial court and to arrive at an independent conclusion as to whether the said evidence can be relied upon or not. In fact, as aforenoted, court(s), while exercising appellate power is not required to consider the question of law, rather, also question of facts to affirmatively reach a ABHISHEK GOYAL GOYAL Date:
2024.10.16 15:44:59 +0530 conclusion of guilt or innocence of an accused. In fact, it is trite law1 that non-re-appreciation of the evidence on record in an appeal may affect the case of either the prosecution or even the accused. Needless to reemphasize that the appellate court is required to be wary of fact that presumption of innocence of an accused, even extents until an accused is held guilty by the final court of appeal and that such a presumption is neither strengthened by an acquittal nor weakened by a conviction in the trial court. 
10. Ergo, being cognizant of the aforesaid, however, before proceeding with the determination of the rival contentions of the parties, it would be pertinent here to reproduce the legal provisions under law/PCA Act, relevant for present adjudication, as under;

6 12. Remarkably, it is observed from a thorough perusal of the PCA Act that the said enactment was brought into force, inter alia, to prevent infliction of unnecessary pain, suffering or cruelty on animals. In particular, the Act was brought into being, wary of the fact that right to dignified life,
envisaged under Article 21 of ABHISHEK GOYAL GOYAL Date:
2024.10.16 15:45:22 +0530 the Constitution of India, extends even to animals. As a corollary, it was duly appreciated at the time of such enactment that every species,
including animals, have an inherent right to live as well as protected by law and that such honor and dignity, cannot be arbitrarily deprived. Appositely, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Animal Welfare Board of India v. A. Nagaraja, (2014) 7 SCC 547,
while asserting similar sentimentalities, noted as under;
"72. Every species has a right to life and security, subject to the law of the land, which includes depriving its life, out of human necessity. Article 21 of the Constitution,
while safeguarding the rights of humans, protects life and the word "life" has been given an expanded definition and any disturbance from the basic environment which includes all forms of life, including animal life, which are necessary for human life,
fall within the meaning of Article 21 of the Constitution. So far as animals are concerned, in our view, "life" means something more than mere survival or existence or instrumental value for human beings, but to lead a life with some intrinsic worth,
honour and dignity. Animals' well-being and welfare have been statutorily recognised under Sections 3 and 11 of the Act and the rights framed under the Act. Right to live in a healthy and clean atmosphere and right to get protection from human beings against inflicting unnecessary pain or suffering is a right guaranteed to the animals under Sections 3 and 11 of the PCA Act read with Article 51-A(g) of the Constitution. 
Right to get food, shelter is also a guaranteed right under Sections 3 and 11 of the PCA Act and the Rules framed thereunder, especially when they are domesticated. 
The right to dignity and fair treatment is, therefore, not confined to human beings alone, but to animals as well. The right, not to be beaten, kicked, overridden,
overloaded is also a right recognised by Section 11 read with Section 3 of the PCA Act. 
Animals also have a right against human beings not to be tortured and against infliction of unnecessary pain or suffering. Penalty for violation of those rights are insignificant, since laws are made by humans. Punishment prescribed in Section 11(1)
is not commensurate with the gravity of the offence, hence being violated with impunity defeating the very object and purpose of the Act, hence the necessity of taking disciplinary action against those officers who ABHISHEK GOYAL GOYAL Date:
2024.10.16 15:45:26 +0530 fail to discharge their duties to safeguard the statutory rights of animals under the PCA Act." 
(Emphasis supplied)

7 13. Markedly, it is observed from above that Section 11 of PCA Act, defines treatment of animals '
cruelly', in particular sub-clause (d) of Section 11(1) provides2 that if any person conveys or carries,
whether in or upon any vehicle or not, any animal in such a manner or position as to subject it to unnecessary pain or suffering, is treating animals cruelly. In fact, the said provision also prescribes a penalty for any such act, in case of first offence, with a fine, which shall not be less than ten rupees but which may extend to fifty rupees, and in the case of second or subsequent offence committed within a span of three years of the previous offence, "with fine which shall not be less than twenty- five rupees but which may extend to one hundred rupees or with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three months, or with both". Correspondingly, Rule 47(a) of TA Rules mandates obtaining of a certificate from a qualified veterinary surgeon as to fitness of travel of cattle by rail or road and as to the animals/cattle not being found suffering with any infectious or contagious or parasitic diseases, etc. Apposite to further note that Rule 54 of TA Rules mandates arrangement of adequate watering arrangements, sufficient feed and fodder as well as ventilation, enroute, failing which compliance of such mandatory rules/provisions, culpability in terms of Section 38(3) PCA Act may be attracted against such violators/offenders.

"Q1. It is in evidence against you that on 11.06.2016 at about 3.15 am you were carrying nine buffalo calves in Tata ACE vehicle without proper food and water and without proper medical certificate. Further, the legs of the animals were also tied with a rope. The floor of the vehicle on which said animals were standing did not have any raita/fuss in order to provide safety for the said animals. 17. Appositely, the Ld. Trial Court, while reaching the finding of guilt of the appellant under the impugned judgment inter alia noted as under;

10 "12. Coming to the facts to the present case, accused has been caught red-handed carrying as many as 9 buffalo calves in a vehicle bearing no. DL-1LR- 4358 in contravention to the provisions of 11(d) of Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act. PW1 Ct. Kavinder Pal Singh has categorically stated in his testimony that the vehicle in which 9 buffaloes calves were being transported were without proper food and water and further legs of the animals were tied with ropes. Further, he has also stated that space of the said vehicle was very small for carrying these animals. This fact is corroborated by the other members who effected the arrest i.e PW2 and PW3. There is no material contradiction in the testimony of these witnesses, I find their testimony truthful and trustworthy. I find no reason for members of DSPCA to falsely implicate the accused. Although, in examination in chief none of the witnesses have mentioned as to the place where accused was caught but PW2 Ct. Naresh Kishore had clearly mentioned in his cross examination that accused along with vehicle was apprehended at Shastri Park, near Shastri Park Chowk. All the three witnesses have stood firm in their cross examination. All of them clearly identified the accused in the court and so mentioned the registration number of the vehicle in which animals Digitally signed by ABHISHEK ABHISHEK GOYAL GOYAL Date:
2024.10.16 15:45:45 +0530 were being carried. This court is of the opinion that carrying animals by tying their legs with rope in a very small space clearly constitute cruelty to them and subjects them to unnecessary pain and suffering and punishable under section 11(d) of Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act. Further, accused has also violated rules 47(a) of transportation of cattle of the above act by not obtaining a fitness certificate from qualified veterinary surgeon declaring that animals were fit to travel and not suffering from any infectious and contagious diseases etc. Further, the witnesses have clearly deposed that there was no proper food and water for the animals and therefore it is also clear violation of rule 54 of Transportation of Animals Rules 1978. In-fact accused in his SA has clearly admitted that he was driving the aforesaid vehicle and carrying the animals but only disputed the numbers of animals. 
He has also admitted his past three convictions of similar offence within a period of 3 years in his SA. Further, same stands recorded in the court STR register and same were specifically put to accused when charge against was framed by Id. Predecessor on 12.08.2016..."
